20	\newcommand{\norm}[1]{\lVert#1\rVert_\infty}
21	\title{Integer multiplication below \texorpdfstring{$n\log n$}{n log n}}
22	\author{OpenAI}
23	\date{September 23, 2026}
24	\begin{document}
25	\maketitle
26	\begin{abstract}
27	We give a deterministic algorithm that multiplies two $n$-bit integers
28	in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ worst-case time, with
29	$\kappa=2^{-182}$, on one fixed finite-alphabet Turing machine with a
30	fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes. The algorithm is exact
31	for every input length and disproves the $n\log n$ optimality conjecture
32	of Sch\"onhage and Strassen in this model.
33	\end{abstract}
34	\tableofcontents
35	\clearpage
36	\section{Introduction}
37	
38	Sch\"onhage and Strassen proved in 1971 that two $n$-bit integers can
39	be multiplied in $O(n\log n\log\log n)$ time on a multitape Turing
40	machine, and proposed $n\log n$ as the optimal order of growth
41	\cite[Section~1]{SchonhageStrassen1971}. After a sequence of improvements,
42	Harvey and van der Hoeven reached the unconditional $O(n\log n)$ upper
43	bound~\cite{HarveyHoeven2021}. We obtain a strict power saving in the
44	logarithmic factor, in the same fixed finite-tape model. The algorithm
45	uses linear combinations of intermediate data to reduce the cost of
46	both address rearrangement and Fourier-transform layers.
47	
48	For a binary string $x$ of length $n$, let $\operatorname{val}(x)$ be
49	its nonnegative integer value, with the leftmost bit most significant.
50	For $0\le z<2^k$, let $\operatorname{bin}_k(z)$ denote its binary
51	representation padded on the left to length $k$. We consider exact
52	multiplication: on input $x\#y$, with $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$, the output
53	must be $\operatorname{bin}_{2n}(\operatorname{val}(x)\operatorname{val}(y))$.
54	Write $\lg n=\max\{\lceil\log_2 n\rceil,1\}$.
55	
56	\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
57	There is one deterministic Turing machine $A$, with a fixed finite
58	alphabet and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes, that
59	computes this exact product for every $n\ge1$ and every pair of $n$-bit
60	inputs. Its worst-case running time satisfies
61	\[
62	 T_A(n)=O\!\left(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa}\right),
63	 \qquad \kappa=2^{-182}.
64	\]
65	\end{theorem}
66	
67	The bound is asymptotic through all input lengths. The constants and
68	thresholds in the construction are extremely large; the algorithm is
69	intended to establish a bit-complexity bound. The theorem refutes an
70	eventual $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound for every fixed multiplication
71	machine in this model.
72	
73	\subsection{The two tape operations}
74	
75	Splitting the inputs into radix digits reduces multiplication to
76	convolution of short integer coefficients. Our starting point is the
77	Gaussian-resampling reduction of Harvey and van der Hoeven
78	\cite{HarveyHoeven2021}: it replaces the Fourier transforms needed for
79	this convolution by multidimensional transforms whose axis lengths are
80	powers of two. After a further conversion to convolution, one coordinate
81	is stored as the coefficient list of a polynomial modulo $y^r+1$, with $r$ a power of two. Powers of $y$ then
82	serve as roots of unity in the remaining axes, and multiplication by
83	such a root is a signed shift of the coefficient list. These are the
84	synthetic polynomial transforms of Nussbaumer and Quandalle and
85	Nussbaumer~\cite{NussbaumerQuandalle1978,Nussbaumer1980}.
86	
87	In this representation, the transform calculation consists of address
88	rearrangements, signed shifts, and two-point butterfly operations.
89	Scanning an array of $\Theta(n)$ stored bits at each of
90	$\Theta(\log n)$ transform levels already costs $\Theta(n\log n)$.
91	We therefore need savings in both movement and arithmetic. Two tape
92	procedures supply them; in both bounds, $V$ denotes the stored bit volume.
93	
94	The first procedure interchanges two disjoint contiguous address fields
95	of $u$ bits in an array whose addresses form a complete Cartesian
96	product. Its cost is $O(Vu^\tau)$ for a fixed $\tau<1$.
97	Although its final effect is an exact permutation, its intermediate
98	steps form pointwise XOR combinations of data. The final permutation is
99	exact for arbitrary initial auxiliary values.
100	
101	The second procedure applies
102	\[
103	 H_0(u,v)=\bigl((u+v)/2,(u-v)/2\bigr)
104	\]
105	simultaneously on selected coordinate bits of the numerical arrays.
106	Each record is a polynomial with complex fixed-point coefficients, and
107	$H_0$ acts coefficientwise. On the layouts used in the multiplication
108	algorithm, one selects the same bit position in each of at most $d$
109	equal-width address chunks, and the cost is $O(Vd^{\lambda'})$ for a
110	fixed $\lambda'<1$. Intermediate values are exact Gaussian dyadics,
111	whose real and imaginary parts have power-of-two denominators. A single
112	truncation follows the completed contractive layer.
113	Section~\ref{sec:tape-interchange} proves the address bound, and
114	Section~\ref{sec:fast-butterfly-layers} gives the numerical layout,
115	precision hypotheses, and layer bound.
116	
117	\subsection{Linear networks and the recursive saving}
118	
119	Each procedure arises from its own fixed linear network that exchanges two
120	banks of values, with prescribed signs, and restores every auxiliary
121	value. A wire's fixed place in the network is called its role. To use
122	the network on an array, regard a row as the complete ordered suffix,
123	including all active address fields, at a fixed prefix and row index.
124	Distribute rows cyclically among the $W$ roles, padding the row count
125	for each prefix to a multiple of $W$. Let $V$ now denote the node volume
126	after padding. All role streams have the same local address set and each
127	contains $V/W$ bits. A scalar gate is then applied
128	pointwise to matching addresses on the roles that it touches.
129	
130	The representation of a role's array may change along the network.
131	At a source, gate, or sink $v$, choose an invertible linear operator
132	$D_v$ on the space of arrays indexed by the common address set. We call $D_v$ its frame: the stored
133	array is $D_vg$ when the logical array is $g$. All incidences of one
134	gate have the same frame. Along an edge from $u$ to $v$, the operator
135	$D_vD_u^{-1}$ changes the stored array from $D_ug$ to $D_vg$.
136	At a pointwise linear gate $G$, the common frame commutes with the gate:
137	\[
138	 G(D_vg_1,\ldots,D_vg_t)=D_vG(g_1,\ldots,g_t).
139	\]
140	The supplied input needs no preliminary change of frame: its logical
141	interpretation is defined by applying the inverse input frame. Thus the
142	intermediate frames cancel, and a route from input role $w$ to output
143	role $\rho(w)$ applies
144	$D_{\mathrm{sink}(\rho(w))}D_{\mathrm{source}(w)}^{-1}$, together with
145	its prescribed scalar sign. Undoing the role exchange and those signs
146	leaves the endpoint operator on every role array, including the roles
147	that carried auxiliary scalar values.
148	
149	For the bit procedure, that endpoint operator is an address shear:
150	two fields, written as vectors $H,D$ over a common residue ring, are
151	updated by $(H,D)\mapsto(H+D,D)$. Two further linear-cost address
152	updates complete their interchange. For the numerical procedure, the
153	endpoint operator becomes the simultaneous $H_0$ layer after diagonal
154	phase operations and a dyadic scale. The intermediate frames are chosen
155	so that every edge can be implemented by smaller calls to the same
156	procedure.
157	
158	The finite construction in Section~\ref{sec:finite-networks} attaches
159	subspaces of a fixed $m$-dimensional space to its gates and terminals.
160	The subspaces at adjacent vertices are nested. Their dimension changes
161	count the smaller operations needed on an edge, with an additional
162	source contribution in the bit construction. The construction uses
163	three-element subsets: gather and scatter create coefficients depending
164	on intersection size, and auxiliary wires cancel the unwanted
165	coefficients. Orthogonality of the corresponding indicator vectors permits
166	the subspace assignments. The decisive property is that the total
167	number $s$ of smaller calls satisfies $s<Wm$.
168	
169	A recursive call at parameter $mf$ therefore uses $s$ calls at parameter
170	$f$, each on a stream of volume $V/W$. The parameter counts field
171	digits for address interchange and selected axes for a numerical layer.
172	After dividing cost by volume, multiplying the parameter by $m$
173	increases the recursive contribution by $s/W<m$. This strict inequality
174	is the source of the power saving. The later tape and arithmetic
175	estimates preserve it, including the work of changing numerical address
176	coordinates. Those changes are implemented by whole-chunk moves and
177	controlled shifts, followed by a deterministic correction of the
178	explicitly identified exceptional addresses.
179	
180	\subsection{From transforms to the exact product}
181	
182	The remaining proof places these procedures inside the multiplication
183	reduction and accounts for every change of representation.
184	First, the radix-digit coefficient list is placed on a product of
185	distinct prime cyclic axes by a Chinese-remainder map that preserves
186	convolution. Section~\ref{sec:assembly} implements this map through
187	triangular controlled shifts and charged axis moves. Gaussian
188	resampling then expresses each source Fourier transform through a
189	power-of-two tensor transform. Section~\ref{sec:resampling} retains the
190	source and target coordinate permutations in the transform identity,
191	so they need not be executed as separate full sorts.
192	
193	Next, Bluestein's chirp identity converts the middle transform,
194	including its target permutation, into normalized cyclic convolution.
195	A phase twist changes the last cyclic coordinate into a polynomial
196	modulo $y^r+1$; its negative wrap gives precisely the original cyclic
197	wrap after the twist is removed. Sections~\ref{sec:synthetic-layouts}
198	and~\ref{sec:exact-ring-products} compute convolution on the remaining
199	axes over this polynomial ring. The two forward synthetic transforms
200	retain the same frequency order through their pointwise product, and
201	the opposite transform consumes that order. Their polynomial products
202	use signed packing and the established $O(n\log n)$ multiplier as an
203	ordinary subroutine.
204	
205	Finally, the source permutation retained during resampling cancels
206	across the two forward source transforms, their pointwise product,
207	and the opposite-sign transform. Section~\ref{sec:assembly} removes
208	the known normalizations and digit scales, proves that the recovered
209	coefficient error is strictly below $1/2$, and propagates carries to
210	obtain the exact binary product. A compatible choice of rational
211	parameters makes all terms in its cost table fit Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
212	Figure~\ref{fig:multiplication-flow} summarizes these reductions.
213	
214	\begin{figure}[ht]
215	\centering
216	\begin{tikzpicture}[
217	 node distance=10mm,
218	 every node/.style={font=\small},
219	 box/.style={draw,rounded corners=2pt,align=center,text width=9.6cm,inner sep=5pt},
220	 >=Stealth]
221	\node[box] (digits) {Integer product\\radix-digit convolution};
222	\node[box,below=of digits] (prime) {Cyclic convolution on distinct prime axes};
223	\node[box,below=of prime] (power) {Normalized convolution on power-of-two axes};
224	\node[box,below=of power] (ring) {Convolution over $\mathbb C[y]/(y^r+1)$\\
225	synthetic transforms and packed polynomial products};
226	\draw[->] (digits)--node[right,font=\scriptsize,align=left]
227	 {Chinese-remainder\\address map}(prime);
228	\draw[->] (prime)--node[right,font=\scriptsize,align=left]
229	 {Gaussian resampling\\and chirps}(power);
230	\draw[->] (power)--node[right,font=\scriptsize,align=left]
231	 {last-coordinate\\phase twist}(ring);
232	\end{tikzpicture}
233	 \caption{The reductions connecting the tape procedures to multiplication.
234	The arrows describe changes of problem and representation. Fast address
235	interchanges organize the layouts, and simultaneous butterfly layers
236	accelerate the synthetic transforms. Solving the final polynomial-ring
237	convolution evaluates the transforms needed in the preceding stages.
238	Known rescalings, rounding, and carry propagation then recover the exact
239	integer product.}
240	\label{fig:multiplication-flow}
241	\end{figure}
242	
243	\subsection{Other arithmetic operations}
244	
245	\begin{corollary}[Exact division and integer square root]
246	\label{cor:exact-arithmetic}
247	There are deterministic machines with fixed finite alphabets and fixed
248	finite numbers of one-dimensional tapes performing the following tasks
249	in $O(n(\lg n)^{1-\kappa})$ worst-case time, for every $n\ge1$. For
250	$x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$, put $a=\operatorname{val}(x)$ and
251	$b=\operatorname{val}(y)$. If $b>0$, the division machine takes $x\#y$
252	and returns $\operatorname{bin}_n(q)\#\operatorname{bin}_n(r)$, where
253	$q=\lfloor a/b\rfloor$ and $r=a-bq$. The square-root machine takes $x$
254	and returns $\operatorname{bin}_n(\lfloor\sqrt a\rfloor)$.
255	Leading zeroes are allowed, and $\kappa$ is as in
256	Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
257	\end{corollary}
258	
259	The classical Newton reductions described by
260	Brent~\cite[Lemmas 2.1--2.4]{Brent1976} compute reciprocal and
261	square-root approximations at geometrically increasing precisions.
262	Their multiplication costs are bounded by a geometric sum controlled by
263	the last precision, and exact remainder and square tests recover the
264	required integer answers. Section~\ref{sec:exact-arithmetic-proof}
265	gives the complete fixed-tape implementation.
266	
267	
268	\subsection{Historical context and inherited methods}
269	
270	Karatsuba's recursive construction, published jointly
271	with Ofman in 1962, gave a binary multiplication circuit of size
272	$O(n^{\log_2 3})$~\cite{KaratsubaOfman1962}. Toom's subsequent use of polynomial
273	evaluation and interpolation gave circuit size
274	$n\exp(O(\sqrt{\log n}))$, and hence $O(n^{1+\eta})$ for every fixed
275	$\eta>0$~\cite{Toom1963}. These early results were formulated in terms of
276	automata and logical networks. Cook adapted Toom's method to the
277	Turing-machine setting; the contemporary account of Sch\"onhage and
278	Strassen credits this adaptation explicitly
279	\cite[Section~1, p.~282]{SchonhageStrassen1971}.
280	
281	In the multitape Turing model,
282	Sch\"onhage and Strassen proved the bound
283	$O(n\log n\log\log n)$ in 1971~\cite{SchonhageStrassen1971}.
284	F\"urer improved it to $n\log n\,2^{O(\log^* n)}$ in 2007, with a full
285	journal account in 2009~\cite{Furer2007,Furer2009}; here $\log^* n$ counts
286	iterated logarithms until a constant threshold is reached.
287	De, Kurur, Saha and Saptharishi developed a modular-arithmetic route to
288	the same scale~\cite{DeKururSahaSaptharishi2013}.
289	Later improvements made the exponential factor $8^{\log^* n}$ and then
290	$4^{\log^* n}$~\cite{HarveyHoevenLecerf2016,HarveyHoeven2019Lattice}.
291	Harvey and van der Hoeven proved the unconditional
292	$O(n\log n)$ bound~\cite{HarveyHoeven2021}.
293	
294	The multitape bounds just cited concern that fixed model. Sch\"onhage obtained
295	linear-time multiplication on storage-modification machines~\cite{Schonhage1980}.
296	Groff later gave a smaller-than-$\log n$ factor in a unit-cost RAM model
297	with constant-time arbitrary memory access, after polynomial preprocessing
298	whose cost is excluded from that bound~\cite[Sections~2 and~4]{Groff2019}.
299	Neither result establishes the bound in the fixed finite-tape model of
300	Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
301	
302	The transform methods behind these bounds also underlie the present
303	construction. Sch\"onhage--Strassen multiplication uses roots of unity in
304	Fermat-type residue rings, where certain multiplications become shifts.
305	F\"urer combines cheap polynomial roots of unity with more general roots,
306	reducing the frequency of expensive multiplications. Harvey and van der
307	Hoeven use Gaussian resampling to pass to multidimensional transforms with
308	power-of-two dimensions, then evaluate them using polynomial transforms
309	developed by Nussbaumer and Quandalle and subsequently by
310	Nussbaumer~\cite{NussbaumerQuandalle1978,Nussbaumer1980,HarveyHoeven2021}.
311	The Gaussian-gridding work of Dutt and Rokhlin is an earlier conceptual
312	precursor~\cite{DuttRokhlin1993}; Harvey and van der Hoeven discuss the
313	connection in~\cite[Section~4.4.3]{HarveyHoeven2021}. The quantitative
314	resampling and bit-cost estimates used here are those of the latter paper.
315	
316	More specifically, the proof adapts Harvey and van der Hoeven's
317	Gaussian-resampling identity, contraction bounds, and short-convolution
318	procedures~\cite[Theorem~4.2, Proposition~4.7 and Lemmas~4.8--4.12]{HarveyHoeven2021}.
319	Their framework already permits arbitrary dimension. Here the source and
320	target permutations remain in the transform identity, while the faster tape
321	procedures perform the required axis movements. Bluestein's conversion to
322	convolution~\cite{Bluestein1970} and the synthetic-root convolution algorithm
323	are retained; the latter follows the polynomial-transform construction
324	in~\cite[Section~2.4 and Section~3]{HarveyHoeven2021}. Signed coefficient
325	packing is a form of Kronecker substitution, with the fixed-tape version
326	of~\cite[Lemma~2.5]{HarveyHoeven2021} as a direct antecedent.
327	Calls to the established $O(n\log n)$ multiplier are ordinary subroutine
328	calls; they do not invoke the improved theorem recursively.
329	
330	\subsection{The finite-network ingredients}
331	
332	The subset-intersection construction in Section~\ref{sec:finite-networks}
333	has an earlier source outside multiplication. Alon's presentation of the
334	Frankl--Wilson construction~\cite{FranklWilson1981} gives low-degree
335	representations of complementary intersection graphs over different fields
336	\cite[Section~3, remark after the proof of Theorem~1.1]{Alon1998}.
337	At the prime $p=2$, its subsets have size three and the two polynomial evaluations
338	are the intersection count modulo two and the intersection count minus one.
339	These are the two pairing formulas used here. We change the ground-set
340	size and express the second pairing through a rational bilinear form.
341	
342	The gather and scatter operations, together with the side wires, have the
343	form of linear index-code decoding: a low-rank linear summary gives the
344	wanted coordinate plus contributions from known neighboring coordinates,
345	and those contributions are subtracted. Bar-Yossef, Birk, Jayram and Kol
346	establish the fitting-matrix formulation and this decoder
347	\cite[Section~3, proof of Theorem~5]{BarYossefBirkJayramKol2006}.
348	Lubetzky and Stav treat decoding over other fields and use related
349	intersection representations to separate their possible ranks
350	\cite[Proposition~2.1 and Section~2.3]{LubetzkyStav2009}.
351	These comparisons explain the algebraic role of the two fields here;
352	they do not supply the subspace labels on the subsequent network.
353	
354	Restoring scratch registers with arbitrary initial contents also has a
355	precise precedent. The transparent-computation construction of Buhrman,
356	Cleve, Kouck\'y, Loff and Speelman subtracts an initial register value,
357	performs a computation, adds the resulting value, and reverses the
358	computation~\cite[Section~3]{BuhrmanCleveKouckyLoffSpeelman2014}.
359	Our scratch schedule is the linear-readout version of that construction.
360	The rank reduction used for address shears is a singular-matrix Bruhat
361	factorization: after reversing the coordinate order, Grigor'ev's
362	upper-triangular factors become the two lower-triangular factors needed
363	here~\cite[Appendix~A.2, Proposition~14(c)]{Grigoriev1982}.
364	
365	The finite networks and their labels are proved directly in
366	Section~\ref{sec:finite-networks}. The additional requirements are the
367	three-stage bank exchange, nested subspaces with a strict total rank or
368	dimension deficit, and endpoint frames acting on every role. The tape
369	implementations then turn that deficit into the volume-normalized
370	recurrences of Sections~\ref{sec:tape-interchange}
371	and~\ref{sec:fast-butterfly-layers}, including the costs of addressing,
372	padding, coefficient growth, and finite precision. The cited decoding,
373	restoration, and factorization results provide ingredients; these further
374	properties are established in the present proof.
375	
376	\subsection{Lower-bound scope and matrix transposition}
377	
378	Sch\"onhage and Strassen conjectured $n\log n$ as the optimal order of
379	multiplication cost~\cite[Section~1]{SchonhageStrassen1971}. In the present
380	fixed-tape model, an eventual lower bound for every multiplication machine means that, for
381	each fixed machine $A$, there are constants $c_A>0$ and $N_A$ such that
382	$T_A(n)\ge c_A n\lg n$ whenever $n\ge N_A$.
383	Its negation requires one machine satisfying
384	$\liminf_{n\to\infty}T_A(n)/(n\lg n)=0$.
385	The power saving proved here gives a limit of zero through all input lengths,
386	which is a stronger conclusion.
387	
388	Harvey and van der Hoeven consider a binary transposition machine
389	supplied an integer $m\ge1$ and a $k\times k$ binary matrix, where
390	$k=\lfloor\sqrt m\rfloor$. They proved that if every fixed such machine
391	has worst-case cost $\Omega(m\lg m)$ through all sufficiently large
392	supplied values of $m$, then every fixed multiplication machine has the
393	corresponding eventual lower bound~\cite[Theorem~1.2]{HarveyHoeven2025}.
394	Combining their quantitative reduction~\cite[Corollary~6.2]{HarveyHoeven2025}
395	with Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives a deterministic fixed-tape algorithm
396	that transposes a row-major $k\times k$ binary matrix in
397	$O(k^2(\lg k)^{1-\kappa})$ time, with $\kappa$ as in
398	Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Section~\ref{sec:transposition} proves the more
399	general rectangular-matrix bound.
400	
401	This comparison concerns unrestricted computation on a fixed number of
402	one-dimensional tapes. Our address procedure forms XOR combinations of
403	intermediate data, even though its final effect is a permutation.
404	It therefore lies outside models restricted to moving data without such
405	computations; see~\cite[Section~1.4]{HarveyHoeven2025} for the distinction.
406	
407	\subsection{Companion application to exact Fourier transforms}
408	
409	The complex phase network of Proposition~\ref{prop:complex-motif-interface}
410	is also used in the companion manuscript~\cite[Section~1.1, Theorem~1.1
411	and Corollary~1.2]{OpenAIExactDFT2026}. That manuscript gives a single
412	algorithm for the exact discrete Fourier transform at every positive
413	transform length $n$. As $n\to\infty$, its cost is
414	$O(n(\log n)^{1-10^{-13}})=o(n\log n)$.
415	
416	The cost is measured in an exact complex-register model that assigns unit
417	cost to exact complex field operations. The algorithm accepts every
418	$x\in\mathbb C^n$, with no bound on its entries or on intermediate complex
419	magnitudes. Its computation on the input uses only addition, subtraction,
420	and multiplication by prepared input-independent scalars. The magnitudes
421	of those scalar coefficients are unrestricted as well.
422	
423	Integer operations and random access on $O(\log(n+2))$-bit words have unit
424	cost, with a fixed number of words for each address or integer. The model
425	supplies one specified Fourier root $\zeta_{D_*}$ of explicitly computable
426	order $D_*<1024n^3$. Scalar preparation, schedule construction, and index
427	work are charged. This is a separate application of the finite network,
428	with its own uniform array implementation. It is neither a bit-complexity
429	consequence nor a stable floating-point FFT consequence of the fixed-tape
430	multiplication theorem, Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
431	  \section{The machine model and elementary streams}
432	\label{sec:streams}
433	
434	A machine has one fixed finite alphabet and one fixed finite number of
435	one-dimensional tapes. A step reads and writes at most one cell on each
436	tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Fixed tracks and finitely
437	many work tapes change time by a fixed factor. We distinguish moving one
438	digit in a fixed radix, which needs a bounded number of scans, from
439	interchanging fields whose numbers of digits grow. The latter permutation
440	will be realized in Section~\ref{sec:tape-interchange} by computing XOR
441	combinations of intermediate data streams. The present section supplies
442	the elementary scans it uses. Every scan includes its counters and the
443	return of its tape heads.
444	
445	\subsection{Array order and elementary scans}
446	
447	For a positive integer $a$ write $[a]=\{0,\ldots,a-1\}$.
448	An array with address set $[a_1]\times\cdots\times[a_t]$ is stored in
449	lexicographic order, with the first coordinate most significant.  Its
450	entries are bits unless a record width is specified.  A trailing record
451	of $B$ bits can equivalently be regarded as a final address field $[B]$.
452	An address is implicit in an entry's position in this ordered stream; it
453	is not stored beside every data bit.
454	The \emph{logical volume} $V$ is the number of stored data bits.  Work
455	tapes and duplicate streams are charged in time but do not increase $V$
456	in recurrences.  All the fields discussed below are nonempty.  A call
457	with an empty array is handled directly.
458	
459	An address permutation $f$ moves the entry at $x$ to $f(x)$.  Thus its
460	action on an array $A$ is $(fA)(f(x))=A(x)$.  Adjacent fields which are
461	irrelevant to an operation may be replaced by a single field whose length
462	is their product.  In particular, the elementary procedures below have a
463	fixed number of formal address fields even when a surrounding algorithm
464	has a growing list of coordinates.  Lengths and positions are supplied in
465	canonical binary on descriptor tapes; no additional tape head is attached to an
466	address coordinate. Each elementary call receives a fixed number of
467	collapsed canonical lengths. Constructing them from a longer surrounding
468	list is work of the caller; recursive calls below construct their own
469	collapsed descriptors within their stated bounds.
470	
471	When one address field is designated as a row field, collapse the fields
472	before it to a prefix $[P]$ and those after it to a suffix $[B]$.  If the
473	row field has range $[R]$, a \emph{row} at prefix $p$ and row index $r$
474	is the complete consecutive block $\{p\}\times\{r\}\times[B]$.
475	Every row therefore contains $B$ bits in the same suffix order.
476	
477	For headers that concatenate a list of positive integer parameters, we use
478	the self-delimiting code
479	\begin{equation}
480	 b_v=\lfloor\log_2v\rfloor+1,\qquad
481	 \Gamma(v)=0^{b_v-1}\operatorname{bin}_{b_v}(v),\qquad
482	 |\Gamma(v)|=2b_v-1\quad(v\ge1).
483	 \label{eq:integer-descriptor-code}
484	\end{equation}
485	The initial zeroes specify how many further bits follow the first one,
486	so concatenated codes can be read in order. We use this code when an
487	interface specifies a header; elementary calls still receive the fixed
488	number of canonical binary lengths described above.
489	
490	\begin{lemma}[Elementary stream operations]
491	\label{lem:elementary-streams}
492	Fix a radix $q\ge2$.  Each of the following operations on an array of
493	volume $V$ takes $O(V)$ steps on a fixed number of one-dimensional tapes:
494	\begin{enumerate}
495	\item any fixed permutation of the pair of digit values at two specified
496	radix-$q$ positions, whether or not the positions are adjacent;
497	\item moving one specified radix-$q$ digit to another position, preserving
498	the order of the intervening positions;
499	\item splitting on a specified radix-$q$ digit, applying a fixed
500	pointwise map to aligned streams, and merging them back;
501	\item for positive integers $P,R,B$, within each prefix of an array on
502	$[P]\times[R]\times[B]$, splitting
503	whole rows cyclically into a fixed number $W$ of streams, and, when $W$
504	divides $R$, merging those streams in any fixed order of the row classes.
505	\end{enumerate}
506	The bounds include shape preparation, counter initialization and resets,
507	and returning or clearing the visited portions of work tapes.  Their
508	constants may depend on the fixed radix, the fixed pointwise map, and the
509	fixed number of row classes.
510	\end{lemma}
511	
512	\begin{proof}
513	For the first operation split into $q^2$ streams according to the two
514	specified digits.  With these digits fixed, the order of all remaining
515	digits is unchanged by the permutation.  Enumerate output addresses in
516	their required order and read the stream prescribed by the two preimage
517	digits.  For a digit move use $q$ streams instead.  The same observation
518	shows that splitting on one digit gives streams with the same remaining
519	address set in the same order.  Scan their aligned entries, apply the
520	fixed pointwise map, and merge according to the output digit; this proves
521	the third operation.  For the fourth, write $r=Wg+w$, where
522	$0\le w<W$, and send the whole row to stream $w$.  If $W$ divides $R$,
523	each stream has address set $[P]\times[R/W]\times[B]$, indexed by the
524	prefix, $g$, and the unchanged suffix.  Thus the streams have the same
525	shape and each has volume $V/W$.  The inverse merge, with any fixed
526	permutation of the classes, reads them in the specified cyclic order.
527	
528	Here are the counter details used in these scans and later ones.  A
529	binary counter is stored with its head at the least significant end.
530	For a counter of width $w$, incrementing or decrementing and returning
531	this head over $L$ consecutive counts costs $O(L+w)$: the number of
532	visits to position $j$ is $O(1+L/2^j)$. The width term is paid when
533	initializing the counter and is absorbed by its complete range scan.  A countdown of
534	length $L$ can be initialized, reset, and tested for underflow in
535	$O(\log(2L))=O(L)$ time.  Keep a local copy of its length on a dedicated
536	track, so a reset does not search a larger descriptor.  For a nested scan
537	of a fixed number of nonempty ranges, the reset of a range is charged to
538	the scan of that range.  Induction on the number of ranges therefore gives
539	linear total counting cost.  A fixed number of empty pieces in a split
540	can be charged to the adjacent nonempty combined range.
541	
542	Only a fixed number of collapsed lengths are needed.  Computing these
543	lengths and the initial counter values by ordinary binary arithmetic
544	takes $O((\log(2V))^C)$ steps for a fixed $C$.  This is $O(V)$ uniformly
545	in $V\ge1$, after increasing a fixed constant.  Each stream is scanned a
546	fixed number of times, and every rewind, copy, or erasure is over a
547	region whose length was charged to that scan.  Delimiters and the fixed
548	number of tracks require only a fixed alphabet enlargement.
549	\end{proof}
550	
551	The next operations are linear because their target field follows their
552	control fields.  This order will be preserved whenever they are invoked.
553	
554	\begin{lemma}[Controlled shifts and fixed rational scalings]
555	\label{lem:ordered-affine-streams}
556	Fix a prime $q$, a fixed number of control fields, and finitely many
557	rational coefficients whose denominators are prime to $q$.  Whenever a
558	coefficient is used as a unit, also require its numerator to be prime to
559	$q$.  Put $Q=q^b$, $b\ge1$.
560	Suppose a target field $y\in[Q]$ follows its control fields, each control
561	used in an offset having $O(b)$ digits.  An update
562	\[
563	 y\longmapsto y+a(\text{controls})\pmod Q
564	\]
565	costs $O(V)$ if the offset can be prepared in $b^{O(1)}$ time from the
566	fixed number of control values.  In particular, this holds for a fixed
567	rational linear combination of them, specialized modulo $Q$.
568	Multiplication of $y$ by any of the specified rational units, and its
569	inverse, also costs $O(V)$.  Arbitrarily long intervening spectator
570	fields and suffix records are permitted.
571	\end{lemma}
572	
573	\begin{proof}
574	Fix all fields before the target, and let the suffix length be $B$ bits.
575	The resulting fiber consists of $Q$ consecutive blocks of length $B$.
576	For an offset $a\in[Q]$, split these blocks at $Q-a$.  Append the two
577	pieces to two tapes, doing so successively for all prefix fibers.  In the
578	merge read the second piece and then the first piece for each prefix.
579	The pieces have become the two consecutive ranges $[0,a)$ and $[a,Q)$
580	of the new target coordinate.  Recompute $a$ when starting that prefix in
581	the merge.  Initializing these two piece lengths and returning the heads
582	of the relevant control counters is included in the $b^{O(1)}$ offset
583	work.  Since
584	\[
585	 b^C=O(q^b)=O(Q)
586	\]
587	for each fixed $C$, this work is absorbed by the $QB\ge Q$ bits of the
588	fiber.  Unrelated spectator counters are incremented by ripple counting;
589	their entire contents are not consulted when computing the offset.
590	
591	For positive fixed integer $c$ prime to $q$, the permutation
592	$y\mapsto cy\pmod Q$ has $c$ increasing pieces, classified by
593	\[
594	 j=\left\lfloor\frac{cy}{Q}\right\rfloor,
595	 \qquad 0\le j<c.
596	\]
597	Prepare their endpoints once for this $Q$, split each fiber into these
598	$c$ streams, and enumerate the output coordinate $y'=0,\ldots,Q-1$.
599	The required stream is the unique $j\in[c]$ for which
600	$y'+jQ\equiv0\pmod c$.  Uniqueness follows from $\gcd(Q,c)=1$;
601	the corresponding $y=(y'+jQ)/c$ lies in $[Q]$.  The stream choice is
602	maintained by a finite residue counter.  Reversing the roles of this
603	split and merge implements multiplication by $c^{-1}$ modulo $Q$.
604	
605	Negation leaves the block at zero fixed and reverses the order of the
606	other $Q-1$ blocks.  Push these blocks consecutively to a temporary tape.
607	Popping gives their order reversed, but also reverses the bits in each
608	block.  Reverse each popped block on a second temporary tape before
609	writing it, restoring its internal order.  Every bit is moved a bounded
610	number of times.  The same procedure is repeated for successive fibers;
611	the temporary stack is emptied and its head returned locally.  A signed
612	rational unit is a composition of these integer multiplications, inverse
613	multiplications, and possibly negation.  Its description is fixed.
614	
615	The nested scan and reset analysis of
616	Lemma~\ref{lem:elementary-streams} applies to all these operations.  In
617	particular, copying a suffix-length counter at every target position
618	costs $O(\log(2B))\le O(B)$ at that position.  It does not introduce a
619	factor $\log V$ per bit.
620	\end{proof}
621	
622	When coefficients have a denominator $d$ prime to $q$, their reductions
623	modulo $q^b$ can be computed by the extended Euclidean algorithm using
624	ordinary tape arithmetic.  The dimension and all original coefficients
625	are fixed, so these preparations have polynomial cost in $b$.  Nothing
626	in Lemma~\ref{lem:ordered-affine-streams} assumes unit-cost arithmetic.
627	
628	For later use, fixed-width signed fixed-point binary addition,
629	subtraction, sign change, and multiplication or division by a fixed
630	power of two are streaming operations of linear bit cost, provided
631	enough integer and fractional guard bits have been allocated for exact
632	results. If an input record is most-significant-bit first, reverse it onto
633	the arithmetic work tape. With least significant bits first on that tape,
634	propagate carries using finite control. Reverse the completed record if
635	its required external order is opposite.
636	This convention separates the order of bits inside a record from the
637	lexicographic order of records. Each required reversal is a linear pass
638	and is charged.
639	 \section{Two finite networks with a rank saving}
640	\label{sec:finite-networks}
641	
642	We construct two fixed linear networks that exchange two banks of values
643	while restoring every auxiliary value.  When the values are replaced by
644	arrays, a common representation on all wires at a gate lets that gate act
645	pointwise without disturbing the representation.  We explain this invariant
646	before constructing the subspace labels that make changes of representation
647	cheap.  The first network uses bit values and rational subspaces; the second
648	uses Gaussian dyadic values and binary subspaces.  The scalar domain specifies
649	the values combined at a gate, while the subspace labels are used to construct operators
650	on each wire's address-indexed array.
651	
652	Put
653	\[
654	 h=100,\qquad v=\binom h3=161700,\qquad
655	 N=v^3=4227952113000000,\qquad m=h^3=1000000.
656	\]
657	Let $\mathcal T$ be the set of three-element subsets of $[h]$.
658	There are two data banks $X_a,Y_a$, indexed by
659	$a=(a_1,a_2,a_3)\in\mathcal T^3$.
660	A wire carries one scalar.  A gate is a fixed linear map on a specified
661	set of wires; untouched wires retain their values.  The vertices on a
662	wire are its source, the gates that touch it in time order, and its sink;
663	its edges join consecutive vertices.  We call the name of a wire its
664	\emph{role}, so that we can distinguish a fixed place in the network
665	from the value currently carried there.
666	
667	\subsection{Scalar operations and restored auxiliary values}
668	
669	There are three stages.  At stage $j$, fix the other two coordinates and
670	operate on the $v$ values in each bank obtained by varying coordinate $j$.  Thus
671	there are $v^2$ separate invocations at each stage.
672	Each such invocation has its own auxiliary wires, distinct from all
673	other invocations, including those in other stages.  There are
674	\[
675	 I=3v^2=78440670000
676	\]
677	invocations.  In a forward invocation, write $x_T$ for the data used as
678	controls and $y_S$ for the data to be updated; $S,T\in\mathcal T$ are
679	their varying $j$th coordinates.  These are the logical source and
680	target banks of the invocation.  For each ordered pair $(S,T)$ that is
681	neighboring under the rule below, there is an auxiliary wire $A_{ST}$.
682	There are also central wires $C_i$, $i\in[h]$, and in the second
683	construction a wire $C_\ast$.  We call all these auxiliary wires
684	\emph{scratch wires}; their initial values may be arbitrary.
685	
686	The following maps specify the construction.
687	\begin{itemize}
688	\item In the bit construction, scalars lie in $\mathbb F_2$, and
689	$S,T$ are neighbors when $|S\cap T|=1$.
690	The copy map adds $x_T$ to $A_{ST}$ for each neighbor pair.
691	The side injection adds $\sum_{T:\,|S\cap T|=1}A_{ST}$ to $y_S$.
692	The gather adds $\sum_{T\ni i}x_T$ to $C_i$, and the scatter adds
693	$\sum_{i\in S}C_i$ to $y_S$.
694	\item In the complex construction, scalars lie in
695	$\mathbb Z[i,1/2]$, and neighbors are distinct triples with even
696	intersection.  Copy is unchanged.  Side injection adds
697	\[
698	 -\sum_{T\text{ neighboring }S}\frac{|S\cap T|-1}{2}A_{ST}
699	\]

\section{Resampling with the permutations left in the transform}
\label{sec:resampling}

The transform lengths needed for the integer product are pairwise coprime,
whereas the synthetic transforms use powers of two. Gaussian resampling
connects these two shapes. Its usual implementation sorts twice on each
coordinate. We retain both permutations in the transform formula and
compute that formula directly. This section proves the resulting interface,
including its tape cost when the number of coordinates grows.

For an integer $q\geq 1$, write
\[
 (F_q u)_k=\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}u_j e^{-2\pi i jk/q},
 \qquad
 (F_q^+ u)_k=\frac1q\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}u_j e^{2\pi i jk/q}.
\]
All subscripts on a vector of length $q$ are taken modulo $q$.
The vector norm is the maximum modulus of its coordinates. All operator
norms are induced by this norm: $\|L\|=\sup_{\|u\|\leq1}\|Lu\|$.
Each normalized Fourier transform above is a contraction, since each
output averages inputs multiplied by complex numbers of modulus one. Coordinate
permutations preserve the norm.
For an integer precision $p\geq1$, put
\[
 \mathbb D_p=\{2^{-p}(a+ib):a,b\in\mathbb Z,\ a^2+b^2\leq 2^{2p}\}.
\]
For storage between completed scalar routines, put $w_{\rm c}=p+2$.
Represent $2^{-p}(a+ib)\in\mathbb D_p$ by a signed $w_{\rm c}$-bit
two's-complement word for $a$, followed by one for $b$, with each word
written most significant bit first. A coordinate list is the
concatenation of these fixed-length records in its stated order. Since
$|a|,|b|\leq2^p<2^{w_{\rm c}-1}$, this format includes both signs of
every permitted numerator, including $-2^p$ and $2^p$.
An approximation $\widetilde L:\mathbb D_p^a\to\mathbb D_p^b$
to a linear contraction $L:\mathbb C^a\to\mathbb C^b$ has error $E$
if $2^p\|\widetilde L u-Lu\|<E$ for every input in $\mathbb D_p^a$.
The approximation itself need not be linear. Composing such algorithms
adds their errors: at each step, insert the exact map at the computed
input and use its contraction bound on the accumulated input error.

We use the established $O(N\log N)$ integer multiplier of
Harvey and van der Hoeven~\cite[Theorem~1.1]{HarveyHoeven2021}
for the shorter integer records that occur below. We also use their
Lemma~2.12: for integer precision $p>100$ and integers $k>1$, $0\leq j<k$,
one can compute $\widetilde\zeta\in\mathbb D_p$ with
$2^p|\widetilde\zeta-e^{2\pi i j/k}|<2$ in time
$O(\max(p,\log k)^{1+\delta})$, for every fixed $0<\delta<1/8$.
Throughout this section, numbered citations to that paper refer to its
author-hosted 45-page manuscript.

\subsubsection{Prime source lengths}

The distinct prime lengths $s_i$ must be close to the powers of two
$t_i$: their product must occupy a fixed fraction of the padded box,
while each ratio $t_i/s_i$ must leave enough separation for resampling.
We verify both requirements for the parameters just chosen.

The prime-interval result
\cite[Lemma~5.1]{HarveyHoeven2021}, based on explicit estimates of
Rosser and Schoenfeld~\cite{RosserSchoenfeld1962}, gives the following
bound: for
$0<\eta<1/4$ and $x>e^{2/\eta}$, the interval
\[
 (1-2\eta)x<q\leq(1-\eta)x
\]
contains at least $\eta x/(2\log x)$ primes. Here $\log$ is the natural
logarithm. The size bounds in \eqref{eq:sizes} give
$d=\Theta(p^\epsilon)$ and $\log r=\Theta(p/d)$.
For large $n$ we have $d\geq2$, so
$0<\eta<1/4$, and
\[
 \frac{\log(r/2)}d=\Theta(p^{1-2\epsilon})\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
----
The machine finds these primes by scanning the two intervals
deterministically and testing each candidate by trial division through
its square root. Testing every candidate would visit $O(r)$ candidates
and at most $O(\sqrt r)$ trial divisors per candidate. Elementary
division on $O(\log r)$-bit integers and management of a list of at most
$d$ selected primes give the conservative bound
$O(dr^{3/2}\operatorname{poly}(p))$. Its logarithm is
\[
 O(\log p+\log r)=O(\log p+p/d)=o(p).
\]
Since $p=6\lceil\log_2 n\rceil=\Theta(\log n)$, the search takes
$n^{o(1)}=o(n)$ time.
All remaining scalar setup, including comparisons for fixed rational
